claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy containing dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The intervention consists of deformation at 600–700 °C to a total strain of approximately 2–3 followed by brief partial annealing at 600–800 °C.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment will disrupt and refine lamellar colonies without causing full recrystallization.
The treatment will produce refined lamellae containing stabilized dislocation substructures.
The refined microstructure will contain smaller boundaries that arrest cracks.
Partial transformation and controlled lamellar refinement reduce stress concentrations.
Partial transformation and controlled lamellar refinement enhance cohesive boundary strength.
Reduced stress concentrations and stronger boundaries retard early microcrack formation.
Retarding microcrack formation promotes more uniform room-temperature deformation and improved ductility.
Lamellar refinement raises the yield stress.
The processed alloy will have a room-temperature yield strength at least 10% greater than the unmodified as-cast baseline.
The processed alloy will have total room-temperature tensile elongation greater than 10%.
The proposed treatment will simultaneously improve strength and ductility relative to the as-cast baseline.
The unprocessed as-cast baseline has coarse lamellar colonies.
The unprocessed as-cast baseline is prone to microcracking and brittle fracture at low tensile strains.
Overlong or excessive annealing coarsens the lamellae.
Annealing-induced coarsening degrades the beneficial strength–ductility microstructure.
Alloy-composition variations affect the achievable strength–ductility combination.
The hypothesis is to be tested by comparing identically tested processed and unprocessed specimens using tensile testing and electron microscopy.
Failure to obtain either a yield-strength increase of at least 10% or total elongation of at least 10% is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the treatment staged warm/cold deformation at 600–700 °C, whereas the intervention specifies only moderate-temperature forging or rolling at 600–700 °C and does not define a distinct cold-deformation stage.
The prediction requires elongation greater than 10%, but the falsification rule triggers only when elongation is below 10%; an outcome exactly equal to 10% would satisfy neither formulation.
